Repairs need the least equipment and build the habits that alterations and making depend on: straight stitching, neat finishing and careful pressing. This course moves in that order. By the end you will repair, alter and make one simple item to a standard you can charge for.
Woven and knit: the first thing to check

**Woven fabric** is made from threads crossing at right angles, like a mat. Ankara (cotton wax print), shirting, denim, guinea brocade, linen and most uniforms are woven. Woven fabric does not stretch much along its threads, and its cut edges fray. **Knit fabric** is made from loops, like a sweater. T-shirts, jersey gowns, leggings and polo shirts are knits. Knits stretch, and their cut edges usually curl rather than fray.

This matters for every job. Knits need a stitch that can stretch with them, such as a narrow zigzag, and a ballpoint needle that slides between the loops instead of cutting them. Wovens need their raw edges finished so they do not fray in the wash. To test, pull the fabric gently: if it stretches easily and springs back, it is a knit.

Before you accept any garment, look at its care label if it has one. It tells you the fibre (cotton, polyester, viscose, a blend) and how hot it can be ironed. Cotton and linen take a hot iron; polyester and viscose need a cooler setting or they shine and melt. Lace and fabrics with sequins or stones should be pressed from the wrong side through a cloth.
Grain: why fabric hangs straight or twists
**Selvedge**: the firm, finished edge on each side of the fabric as it comes off the roll. It does not fray.
**Straight grain (lengthwise grain)**: runs parallel to the selvedge. It is the strongest direction with the least stretch. Most garment pieces are cut with their length on the straight grain.
**Cross grain**: runs from selvedge to selvedge, at right angles to the straight grain. It has a little more give.
**Bias**: any diagonal line; the true bias is at 45 degrees. Woven fabric stretches most on the bias, which is why bias strips curve neatly around necklines.
When you cut a patch or a new piece off grain, it twists after washing and the garment hangs badly. When you repair, try to match the grain of the patch to the grain of the garment.

A sewing machine is fast, but many repairs are done by hand: hems on fine fabric, small seam splits, linings, buttons and anywhere the machine cannot reach. Six hand stitches cover nearly every repair you will meet. Learn them on scrap fabric until your stitches are even in size and spacing.
A sewing needle and thread
Six simple hand stitches handle most everyday repairs.
Getting ready: needle, thread and knot
Cut a piece of thread about 45 to 50 cm long, roughly the length from your fingertips to your elbow and back. Longer thread tangles and wears thin as it passes through the fabric.
Cut the end at a slant with sharp scissors so it passes through the needle eye easily.
Thread the needle. For most repairs use a single thread; for buttons, use a double thread (pull the ends together) for extra strength.
Tie a knot at the end: wrap the thread twice around your index finger, roll it off with your thumb, and pull the loop tight.
Start from the wrong side (inside) of the fabric so the knot is hidden.
Match the needle to the fabric

Use a fine, sharp needle for shirting and lace, a medium needle for ankara and cotton, and a thicker needle for denim. Choose thread a shade darker than the fabric; it blends in better than a lighter one.
The six stitches
Stitch
How you make it
Use it for
Running stitch
Push the needle in and out along a straight line, making stitches and gaps of equal length (about 3 to 5 mm).
Gathering, temporary basting (tacking) before machine sewing, quick light seams
Backstitch
Make one stitch forward, then bring the needle up one stitch length ahead and go back down at the end of the last stitch, so the stitches touch.
The strongest hand seam; mending split seams, crotch and underarm repairs
Slip stitch (ladder stitch)
Take a small stitch inside the fold on one side, then a small stitch inside the fold directly opposite, like rungs of a ladder. Pull gently and the opening closes invisibly.
Closing a gap in a seam from the outside, closing linings, stuffed items
Blind hem stitch
Take a tiny stitch, just one or two threads, from the garment, then a slightly longer stitch inside the folded hem edge. Repeat about every 1 cm.
Hems on trousers, skirts and dresses where stitches must not show on the outside
Whipstitch
Pass the needle over the edge of the fabric and back through from the same side, making slanted stitches.
Joining two finished edges, attaching patches, felt
Overcast stitch
Like whipstitch but worked over a single raw edge, with stitches about 5 mm apart and 5 mm deep.
Stopping a cut edge from fraying when you have no overlocker or zigzag
Finishing so the stitching holds

A line of stitches is only as strong as its ending. On the wrong side, take a tiny stitch through the last stitch but do not pull it tight. Pass the needle through the loop that forms, then pull firmly. Repeat once more, then trim the thread leaving about 5 mm. This is often called a **knot finish** or **locking stitch**. Never end by simply cutting the thread; the stitches will pull out with the first wash.

Worked example: mending a split underarm seam
For example, Halima's neighbour brings a cotton blouse with a 6 cm split in the underarm seam. The fabric itself is not torn; only the stitching has broken.
Halima turns the blouse inside out and pulls out the loose broken threads so they do not get caught.
She pins the two seam edges together along the original stitching line, which she can still see as small holes.
She starts with a knot about 1 cm before the split, in the old stitching that is still good, so the repair overlaps.
She sews backstitch with stitches about 2 to 3 mm long along the old line, ending 1 cm past the split.
She finishes with two locking stitches and trims the thread, then presses the seam.
The repair overlaps sound stitching by 1 cm at each end, so the seam will not split again at the same point. The job takes about 15 minutes.

Speed comes later. At first, aim for stitches of the same length with the same gaps. A useful habit is to count: for a backstitch seam, about three to five stitches per centimetre on light fabric, fewer on thick denim. Even, small stitches look professional and hold far better than long, uneven ones.
Do not sew too tight
Pulling each stitch hard makes the fabric pucker (wrinkle). Pull until the thread lies flat on the fabric and stop there. Check by laying the work flat: it should not ripple.

Good tailoring depends on accurate numbers. A mistake of 2 cm at the waist is the difference between a comfortable fit and a garment that will not close. In this lesson you learn to measure a person and a garment in centimetres, and to set up a work corner that keeps you, your family and your customers' clothes safe.

Allowances: the extra fabric beyond the stitching line

**Seam allowance** is the distance between the cut edge and the stitching line. Many commercial patterns use 1.5 cm; some use 1 cm. When you take in or let out a garment, the seam allowance is the fabric you have to work with. **Hem allowance** is the fabric folded up at the bottom of a garment. For trousers, about 4 cm is common; for a straight skirt, 4 to 5 cm; for a full or curved skirt, a narrow hem of about 1 to 2 cm sits better.
Worked example: measuring for a trouser hem
For example, Bisi brings her son's school trousers to Fatima, a home tailor. They are 6 cm too long. The current hem is 3 cm deep.
Fatima has the boy wear the trousers with his school shoes and folds the hem up until it just touches the top of the shoe at the front.
She pins it and measures from the old hem edge to the new fold: 6 cm.
She decides on a finished hem allowance of 4 cm.
New cutting line = new fold line + 4 cm of hem allowance. She marks the fold line with chalk, then a second line 4 cm below it.
Old fabric below the new fold is 6 cm + 3 cm old hem = 9 cm. She keeps 4 cm and trims off 5 cm.
Fatima knows exactly where to fold and where to cut before she touches the scissors, so there is no risk of cutting too short.
Measure twice, cut once
Fabric cut too short cannot be put back. Pin, check on the person or against a garment that fits, and measure both legs or both sides before cutting.

Good light reduces mistakes and eye strain; sit near a window in the day and use a bright bulb at night. Keep pins and needles in a closed tin, never in your mouth. Pick up dropped pins with a magnet. Keep scissors closed and out of children's reach. An iron is hot enough to burn skin and fabric: stand it upright on its heel, keep the cable away from the edge where a child could pull it, and switch it off at the wall when you finish. When the grid is off and you use a generator, never run it indoors or near windows, because its fumes contain carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas you cannot smell.

Never touch an electric machine or iron with wet hands, and unplug them before cleaning. Run any generator outside, away from doors and windows, to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning.

In Nigeria you will meet three kinds of machines. **Manual machines** are turned by a hand wheel or a foot **treadle** and need no electricity; the Butterfly brand is a common example in local markets. **Electric domestic machines** from brands such as Singer, Janome and Brother run on a foot pedal and often have zigzag and other stitches. **Industrial straight-stitch machines** are fast, heavy machines used in busy tailoring shops. The threading principles are the same on all of them.

Threading the upper thread
Raise the presser foot. This opens the tension discs so the thread can sit between them. If the foot is down, the thread misses the discs and you get a tangle of loops underneath.
Turn the hand wheel towards you until the needle and the take-up lever are at their highest point.
Place the reel on the spool pin and lead the thread through the top thread guide.
Bring the thread down the channel through the tension area, around the U-turn, and up to the take-up lever. Hook it through the lever's eye or slot.
Bring it down through the guides just above the needle.
Thread the needle. On most modern domestic machines this is front to back; some older machines thread from the side. Check your manual.
Pull about 10 to 15 cm of thread through and lay it under the presser foot.
Winding and inserting the bobbin

Wind thread onto an empty bobbin using the bobbin winder on top of the machine, so the thread goes on evenly and firmly. Insert it as your machine requires: a **drop-in bobbin** sits flat under a clear cover beside the needle plate; a **front-loading bobbin** goes into a separate metal bobbin case behind a small door. Hold the upper thread lightly, turn the hand wheel towards you one full turn, and the needle will bring up a loop of bobbin thread. Pull both threads to the back under the foot.
Reading the stitch and fixing tension

In a balanced stitch, the upper and bobbin threads lock between the two fabric layers, and the stitch looks the same on both sides. Set stitch length to about 2.5 mm for normal seams. At the start and end of every seam, sew three or four stitches in reverse to lock it.

Loops underneath: rethread top
Bobbin thread on top: lower top tension
Skipped stitches: change needle
Thread breaks: check reel, needle

Care and maintenance
**Unplug** an electric machine before cleaning or changing the needle.
**Clean** lint from the feed dogs and bobbin area with a small brush after every few hours of sewing. Lint build-up causes skipped stitches and noise.

**Oil** only where your manual shows, with sewing machine oil, never cooking oil. Treadle machines have several oil holes. After oiling, sew on a scrap to absorb any extra oil before touching a customer's garment.

**Change the needle** at the start of each big project, after about 8 hours of sewing, or at once if it is bent, blunt or skipping. On most domestic machines the flat side of the needle shank faces the back.
**Cover** the machine when not in use to keep out dust.

Hemming trousers: the method
Ask the customer to wear the trousers with the shoes they will wear with them. Fold the hem up to the length they want, usually just touching the top of the shoe at the front, and pin.
Measure from the floor or from the old hem to the pinned fold on one leg. Check the other leg on the person too. Never assume both legs are the same length.
Unpick the old hem with a seam ripper and press it flat.
Mark the new fold line with chalk. Measure the hem allowance below it (about 4 cm for trousers) and mark the cutting line. Cut along it.
Finish the raw edge: zigzag, overlock or turn under 1 cm and press.
Fold up on the fold line, press, and pin. Sew with a blind hem stitch by hand, or by machine.
Press again from the wrong side. Check both legs are the same length by folding the trousers in half.

Sewing on a button with a thread shank

A button sewn flat against the fabric is hard to fasten and pulls loose. The fix is a **thread shank**: a short stem of thread between the button and the fabric, about the thickness of the fabric around the buttonhole.
Mark the position by closing the garment and pushing a pin through the buttonhole into the fabric beneath.
Use a double thread with a knot. Bring the needle up from the wrong side at the mark.
Place a pin or matchstick across the top of the button and sew over it, passing up and down through the holes six to eight times. For a four-hole button, sew each pair of holes.
Remove the pin or matchstick and lift the button away from the fabric.
Wrap the thread three or four times tightly around the stitches under the button to form the shank.
Pass the needle to the wrong side and finish with two locking stitches.

Some buttons already have a **shank**: a small loop or stem on the back, common on coats and blazers. Sew these with four to six passes through the loop, keeping the loop in line with the buttonhole so the button does not twist. On a coat or any garment where the button takes strain, sew a small flat button on the inside directly behind it at the same time. This **stay button** spreads the pull so the fabric does not tear. Metal jeans buttons are not sewn at all; they are fixed with a hammer-on tack, and replacement sets are sold in markets.

Patch a tear and darn a small hole

A broken zip can make a good skirt, bag or trouser useless, so customers will pay for a quick, neat replacement. Seam splits, tears and small holes are just as common. In this lesson you learn to judge the damage first, then fix it in the way that will last.
A pair of scissors
Unpicking carefully is half of every zip replacement.
First, diagnose the zip
**Teeth are fine but the zip splits open behind the slider:** the slider is often worn and has spread. Sometimes a new slider of the same size fixes it without removing the zip.
**Teeth are missing or broken, or the tape is torn:** replace the whole zip.
**Pull tab has snapped off:** a replacement pull or a small split ring can be fitted.
**Zip is stiff:** rub a little candle wax or dry soap along the teeth before deciding it is faulty.
Replacing a centred skirt zip

A **centred zip** sits behind a seam with stitching an equal distance on each side of the teeth. It is common on the back seam of skirts and gowns. You need a new zip of the same length (or a little longer), a **zipper foot**, which lets the needle sew close to the teeth, and matching thread.
Before unpicking, photograph the old zip and note where the stitching sits and how the top is finished at the waistband or facing.
Unpick the old zip with a seam ripper. Remove all loose thread ends.
Press the seam allowances back along the original fold lines.
Pin the new zip face down behind the opening, with the teeth exactly centred on the seam line and the top stop just below the waist seam allowance.
Hand baste (tack) with running stitch about 6 mm from the teeth on each side, then remove the pins. Basting stops the zip from shifting.
With the zipper foot, machine stitch down one side, across the bottom just below the bottom stop, and up the other side. Move the slider out of the way as you go.
Remove the basting, close the waistband or facing, and press from the wrong side with a cloth.
Never sew over metal teeth
Sewing across metal teeth or the stops breaks the needle and can throw pieces towards your eyes. Turn the hand wheel slowly by hand near the bottom stop, and keep your face back from the needle.
Mending a split machine seam

Turn the garment inside out. Find where the stitching has broken. Begin machine stitching 1 to 2 cm before the break, on top of the old stitching line, and continue 1 to 2 cm beyond it. Lock both ends. If the seam allowance has frayed away, sew a fraction inside the old line and finish the raw edge with zigzag.
Patching and darning

For a **tear** (a straight or L-shaped rip), place a patch of similar fabric behind it on the wrong side, larger than the tear by about 2 cm on every side, with the grain matching. Turn the patch edges under or zigzag them. Bring the torn edges together on the right side and stitch over them with a small zigzag or many short rows of straight stitching. For a **small hole** in a knit or sock, **darning** weaves new thread across the hole: first a row of parallel stitches in one direction, then weave over and under them at right angles.
Choosing the right fix
Is the damage on a seam?
Yes: restitch seam line
No: tear or hole?
Tear: patch behind
Small hole: darn
Look at where the damage is before choosing a method.
Worked example: zip or slider?
For example, Chioma brings Uche a jeans skirt. The zip teeth are all present, but the zip opens behind the slider when she sits down.
Uche checks the teeth: none missing, tape not torn.
She sees the slider gaps slightly at the back, a sign of wear.
She explains the two options: replace the slider, or replace the whole zip if a matching slider cannot be found.

She finds a slider of the same size number (often stamped on the back of the old slider) at the market, removes the top stops with pliers, slides the new slider on from the top, and fits new top stops.
She tests the zip ten times and tells Chioma it is working.
The repair takes about 20 minutes and costs much less than a full zip replacement. If the slider had not matched, Uche would have replaced the zip.
Buy the right zip
Common zips are nylon coil (light garments), plastic moulded and metal (jeans, bags). Jackets need a separating (open-ended) zip. Take the old zip to the market to match type and length.

Many people own clothes that fit almost right: a gown that is loose at the waist after weight loss, a shirt that is boxy, a skirt that has become tight. Taking in and letting out side seams are the most requested fit alterations. The skill is in the numbers and in a smooth line, so the altered garment looks as if it was made that way.
A dress
A side-seam alteration changes the fit of a dress without changing its style.
The key calculation: every seam counts twice

When you move a stitching line 1 cm inward, you remove 1 cm from the front piece and 1 cm from the back piece at that seam. So the garment becomes **2 cm smaller per seam**. A garment with two side seams becomes 4 cm smaller in total. The rule is: **amount to move each seam = total reduction needed divided by (2 × number of seams you alter)**.

Always alter both side seams by the same amount so the garment stays balanced and the side seams stay at the sides of the body. If more than about 5 cm must come out of each seam, the shape of armholes, pockets or darts may be affected; that is a bigger job and should be priced and discussed as such.
Taking in a side seam: step by step
Have the customer try the garment on, right side out. Pin out the extra fabric evenly at both side seams until it fits comfortably. Let her sit and raise her arms to check it is not too tight.
Measure how much you pinned at the waist, bust and hip. Write the numbers on a job card.
Remove the garment, turn it inside out and mark the new stitching line with chalk, using your measurements from the old seam line.
Taper the new line smoothly back into the old seam over about 8 to 10 cm at the top and bottom of the alteration. A sudden angle makes a visible dent.
Baste (tack) along the new line and do a second fitting. Adjust if needed.
Machine stitch the new line at about 2.5 mm, locking both ends, then remove the old stitches only where they would show on the outside.
If the seam allowance is now very wide, trim it to about 1.5 cm, or leave it if the customer may want it let out later. Finish raw edges and press.
Letting out: check the allowance first

You can only let out as much as the seam allowance allows. Unpick a small section of the side seam on the inside and measure. If the allowance is 2 cm, you can usually let out up to about 1 cm per seam and still keep 1 cm to hold the seam; across two side seams that gives up to 4 cm more room. On dark or shiny fabrics the old stitch holes and fold line may still show. Press with a damp pressing cloth and test on the inside first. Tell the customer honestly before you start if marks may remain.

She marks the new line 1.5 cm inside the old seam at the waist and 1 cm inside at the hip, on both sides.
She tapers the line back to 0 cm about 10 cm above the waist, so the bust is untouched.
She bastes, does a second fitting with Ruth, and finds the fit is right.
She stitches, finishes the edges with zigzag and presses.
The gown is 6 cm smaller at the waist and 4 cm smaller at the hip, with a smooth line and unchanged bust. Adaeze records the numbers on the job card in case Ruth wants it let out again.

Leave extra seam allowance inside the garment until the customer has tried on the finished alteration. You cannot add fabric back once it is cut away.

Quality standards and fixing common sewing faults
Inspect a finished job against a clear quality checklist

Customers judge a tailor by small details: a loose thread, a hem that is longer on one leg, a seam that wrinkles. These are all preventable. A written quality standard, checked on every job before handover, protects your name and brings customers back.
A check mark
Check every job against the same standard before you hand it back.
Your handover quality checklist
**Stitches**: even length (about 2.5 mm for normal seams), balanced on both sides, no loops, no skipped stitches.
**Seams**: straight, at the agreed allowance, locked at both ends, no puckering.
**Symmetry**: both legs, sleeves or sides match within about 0.5 cm.
**Edges**: raw edges finished with zigzag, overlock, overcast or a turned edge, so nothing will fray.
**Fastenings**: buttons, hooks and zips open and close smoothly ten times.
**Finish**: all loose threads trimmed, chalk marks removed, garment pressed and folded or hung.

Finishing raw edges: your options
**Zigzag**: sew a medium zigzag along the raw edge so the right swing of the needle falls just off the edge. Works on most domestic electric machines.

**Overlock (serger)**: a separate machine that trims and wraps the edge with three or four threads in one pass. It is what factory garments use; many tailors pay a neighbour with an overlocker a small fee per garment until they buy one.
**Hand overcast**: slow but needs no machine, ideal for a manual straight-stitch machine user.
**Turned and stitched**: fold the raw edge under about 5 mm and straight stitch it. Neat on light cotton.
**French seam**: sew wrong sides together, trim, then sew again right sides together, enclosing the raw edge. Good for sheer fabric and lace linings.
**Pinking shears**: zigzag-bladed scissors that slow fraying on firm cotton; not enough on loose weaves.

Match the finish to what the garment already has. If the factory edge is overlocked and you have no overlocker, a neat zigzag is an acceptable substitute; tell the customer if the finish will look different inside.
Pressing: the step beginners skip

**Pressing** is not the same as ironing. Ironing slides the iron back and forth; pressing means lifting the iron and setting it down on one area at a time, so the fabric does not stretch. Press each seam flat as sewn first, to set the stitches, then press it open or to one side. Use the right heat for the fibre, and a damp cotton pressing cloth on dark, shiny or delicate fabric to stop shine and scorching. A well-pressed alteration looks professional even when the stitching is simple.

All four pairs pass the checklist. Ten minutes of checking saved her from a complaint and a return visit.

Honest service

Privacy and respect

Fake payment alerts

Deposits and collection

Good work becomes income when it is priced correctly, shown clearly and offered to the right people. In this module you build a price list from real costs, create a before-and-after portfolio and WhatsApp Business catalogue, and complete your capstone with a 90-day plan for your service.

Many beginner tailors set prices by guessing or by copying the cheapest person on the street, then wonder why they work hard and have nothing left. A price must cover four things: the **materials** used, your **time** (labour), your **running costs** (overheads) and a **profit** that lets you save, replace tools and grow.
An abacus
Every price is built from materials, time, running costs and profit.
The four parts of a price
**Materials**: zip, thread, buttons, interfacing, patch fabric. Count only what the job uses; a reel of thread does many jobs.
**Labour**: minutes spent × the value of your time per hour. Decide a fair hourly value and use it consistently.
**Running costs**: generator fuel or electricity, needles, machine oil and servicing, data for WhatsApp, transport to the market. Add them up for a month and share them across your jobs.
**Profit**: an extra percentage on top of costs, often 20 to 30% for small service work. Profit is not the same as your pay; your pay is already in labour.
Sharing monthly running costs

Add up your running costs for a typical month and divide by the number of jobs you usually do. For example, if running costs are about ₦12,000 (approximate) a month and you do about 60 jobs, each job carries about ₦200 of running costs. Recalculate every few months, because fuel and data prices change.

Setting up WhatsApp Business

WhatsApp Business is a free app from WhatsApp for small businesses. It lets you create a business profile with your name, address area, hours and a short description, add a **catalogue** of services with photos and prices, set a greeting message and quick replies, and label chats (for example "new order", "ready for collection"). Use a separate number from your personal one if you can, so work messages stay organised.
**Profile description**: one clear line, for example "Clothing repairs and alterations: hems, zips, buttons, fit. Pick-up in Ikeja."

Know your fabric, sew strong hand stitches, measure right
Know your fabric, sew strong hand stitches, and measure right.
This is the video for module one of Basic Tailoring and Garment Repair.
Why this matters
Three kinds of tailoring work
Repair: bring a damaged garment back to use
Alteration: change the fit or length
Making: cut and sew a new item
Start with repair
Almost every home has clothes waiting for small fixes. A home tailor earns from three kinds of work. Repair brings a damaged garment back to use.
Alteration changes the fit or length of a garment that is already made.
Making means cutting and sewing a new item from fabric.
Start with repair. It needs the least equipment and builds the habits you need later: straight stitching, neat finishing and pressing.
Check first
Woven or knit?
Threads cross like a mat
Barely stretches
Ankara, shirting, denim
Made from loops
Stretches and springs back
Cut edges curl
T-shirts, jersey, leggings
Before any job, check the fabric. Woven fabric is made from threads crossing at right angles, like a mat.
Ankara, shirting and denim are woven. They barely stretch, and their cut edges fray, so you must finish those edges.
Knit fabric is made from loops, like a sweater. T-shirts, jersey gowns and leggings are knits.
To test, pull gently. If it stretches easily and springs back, it is a knit. Knits need a stretchy stitch, such as a narrow zigzag, and a ballpoint needle.
Six hand stitches
The right stitch for the job
Running stitch: basting and light seams
Backstitch: the strongest hand seam
Slip stitch: closes a gap invisibly
Blind hem: hems that must not show
Whipstitch: joins finished edges, patches
Overcast: stops a raw edge fraying
Six hand stitches cover nearly every repair. Running stitch goes in and out in a straight line. Use it for tacking before machine sewing.
Backstitch is the strongest hand seam. Each stitch touches the last. Use it to mend split seams.
Slip stitch, also called ladder stitch, closes an opening from the outside so nobody can see it.
Blind hem stitch picks up just one or two threads of the garment, so the hem does not show on the outside.
Whipstitch passes over the edge to join two finished edges or attach a patch.
Overcast stitch is worked over a single raw edge, to stop fraying when you have no zigzag or overlocker.
Step by step
Mending a split underarm seam
Overlap into good stitching and always lock the end
Turn inside out, pull out broken threads
Pin edges along the old stitching line
Knot 1 cm before the split
Backstitch to 1 cm past the split
Two locking stitches, trim, press
For example, Halima's neighbour brings a cotton blouse with a 6 cm split in the underarm seam. Only the stitching has broken.
Step one. Halima turns the blouse inside out and pulls out the loose broken threads.
Step two. She pins the two edges together along the original stitching line. She can still see it as small holes.
Step three. She starts with a knot about 1 cm before the split, in old stitching that is still good.
Step four. She sews backstitch, with stitches about 2 to 3 mm long, and ends 1 cm past the split.
Step five. She finishes with two locking stitches, trims the thread, and presses the seam.
Never end by simply cutting the thread. The stitches will pull out in the first wash. And do not pull stitches too tight, or the fabric will pucker.
Shortening school trousers
Fold up to touch the top of the shoe
Measure: 6 cm too long
Old hem 3 cm, so 9 cm below the fold
Keep a 4 cm hem allowance
Trim off 5 cm
For example, Bisi brings her son's school trousers to Fatima. He wears them with his school shoes, and Fatima folds the hem up until it just touches the top of the shoe.
She pins and measures. The trousers are 6 cm too long.
The old hem is 3 cm deep. So there is 9 cm of fabric below the new fold.
Trousers usually need a hem allowance of about 4 cm. She marks the fold line with chalk, then a cutting line 4 cm below it.
So she keeps 4 cm and trims off 5 cm. Fabric cut too short cannot be put back, so measure both legs before cutting.

Good light on your work
Needles and pins in a closed box
Scissors closed, out of children's reach
Generator outside, away from windows
Now set up a safe corner, with good light by day and a bright bulb at night.
Keep pins and needles in a closed tin, never in your mouth, and keep scissors closed and away from children.
Stand the iron on its heel, keep its cable away from the edge, and switch it off at the wall when you finish.
Run any generator outside, away from doors and windows. Its fumes contain carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas you cannot smell.
Remember
Key points
Start with repair work
Woven frays; knit stretches and curls
Backstitch is strongest; finish with locks
Measure snug, write in cm at once
Mark fold line and cutting line first
So remember. Start with repairs. Check woven or knit. Backstitch is the strongest hand seam, and every line ends with locking stitches.
Measure snug but not tight, write numbers in centimetres at once, and mark both lines before you cut.

What you will learn

This module is about the jobs customers ask for most. First, you thread your machine and read the stitch it makes.
Then you hem trousers, the same length on both legs.
You sew buttons that fasten easily and stay on.
And you replace zips and mend seams and tears, so they last.
Step by step
Thread with the presser foot UP
Raise the presser foot
Needle and take-up lever at the top
Down through the tension area
Up through the take-up lever
Down the guides and through the needle
Step one. Raise the presser foot. This opens the tension discs so the thread can sit between them.
Step two. Turn the hand wheel towards you until the needle and the take-up lever are at their highest point.
Step three. From the reel, lead the thread through the top guide, then down the channel through the tension area and around the U-turn.
Step four. Bring it up and hook it through the take-up lever. Many tangles come from missing this.
Step five. Bring it down through the guides and thread the needle, then pull 10 to 15 cm through.
If the foot is down while you thread, the thread misses the discs and you get a nest of loops underneath.
Reading the stitch
Three common stitch problems
Usually the upper thread. Raise the foot and rethread the top from the beginning.
The top tension is too tight. Lower the top tension a little.
Change the needle. Clean out lint from the feed dogs and bobbin area.
A balanced stitch looks the same on both sides. Sew normal seams at about 2.5 mm, with three or four reverse stitches at each end.
For example, Ngozi finds loops on the underside. She rethreads the top, and the stitch is balanced. She never touched the tension dial.
If the bobbin thread shows on top, lower the top tension.
Skipped stitches mean change the needle. Change it after about 8 hours of sewing anyway. Unplug the machine before cleaning, and use sewing machine oil, never cooking oil.
Hemming trousers
A hem that matches on both legs
Never assume both legs are the same length
Customer wears the shoes; pin the fold
Measure and check each leg
Unpick old hem; mark fold and cut lines
Finish raw edge; fold, press, pin
Sew blind hem; press and compare legs
Ask the customer to wear the trousers with their shoes. Fold the hem to just touch the top of the shoe at the front, and pin.
Measure one leg, then check the other leg on the person too. Never assume both legs are the same.
Unpick the old hem and press it flat. Mark the new fold line, then a cutting line about 4 cm below it, and cut.
Finish the raw edge with zigzag, or turn it under 1 cm. Fold up, press and pin.
Sew a blind hem so nothing shows outside on office trousers. Jeans get a topstitched machine hem. Press, then fold the trousers in half to check both legs match.
Buttons that stay on
Sewing a button with a thread shank
Mark through the buttonhole with a pin
Double thread with a knot
Sew over a pin, six to eight passes
Wrap the thread to form the shank
Two locking stitches on the wrong side
A button sewn flat is hard to fasten and pulls loose. Close the garment and push a pin through the buttonhole to mark the spot.
Use a double thread with a knot, coming up from the wrong side.
Lay a pin or matchstick across the button and sew over it, six to eight times through the holes.
Remove the pin, lift the button, and wrap the thread three or four times under it. That short stem is the thread shank.
Finish with two locking stitches on the wrong side.
Zips
Diagnose the zip first
New slider
Teeth all fine
Splits open behind slider
Slider worn and gaping
Whole new zip
Teeth missing or broken
Tape torn
No matching slider

If teeth are missing or the tape is torn, replace the whole zip. Baste it first, then sew with a zipper foot.
Never sew over metal teeth or the stops. The needle breaks and pieces can fly towards your eyes, so turn the wheel slowly by hand there.

This is the video for module three of Basic Tailoring and Garment Repair.
Why this matters
From repairs to fit alterations
Clothes that fit almost right
Get the numbers right
Check every job before handover

Many people own clothes that fit almost right. A gown loose at the waist, or a skirt that has become tight. Taking in and letting out side seams are the most requested fit alterations.
The skill is in the numbers, and in a smooth line, so the garment looks as if it was made that way.
Then you check every job against a clear standard before the customer sees it.
And you run each order with a job card, so there are no quarrels about what was agreed.
The key calculation
Every seam counts twice
Two side seams: divide the total reduction by four
Move a seam 1 cm in
Front loses 1 cm, back loses 1 cm
So 2 cm smaller per seam
Two side seams: 4 cm smaller in total
Here is the calculation that matters most. Suppose you move a stitching line 1 cm inward.
You remove 1 cm from the front piece, and 1 cm from the back piece, at that seam.
So the garment becomes 2 cm smaller at that one seam.
With two side seams, it becomes 4 cm smaller in total. So for two side seams, divide the total reduction you want by four.
Always alter both sides by the same amount, so the side seams stay at the sides of the body.
Worked example
Taking in Ruth's ankara gown
Taper into the old seam. A sudden angle makes a dent.
Waist 6 cm too big: 1.5 cm per seam
Hip 4 cm too big: 1 cm per seam
Taper back to 0 cm, 10 cm above waist
Baste and do a second fitting
Stitch, zigzag the edges, press
At the waist, 6 divided by four is 1.5 cm per seam.
At the hip, 4 divided by four is 1 cm per seam. She marks the new line on both sides.
She tapers the line back to nothing about 10 cm above the waist, so the bust is untouched. A smooth taper over about 8 to 10 cm hides the change.
She bastes, which means tacking with loose running stitch, and does a second fitting. The fit is right.
Only then does she machine stitch, finish the edges with zigzag and press. Do not cut away extra allowance until the customer has tried it on. Fabric cannot be added back.
Letting out
Check the allowance first
Allowance 2 cm
Let out up to about 1 cm
Keep 1 cm to hold the seam
Up to 4 cm more room
Be honest
Old holes may still show
Test pressing on the inside
Tell her before you start

To let a garment out, first unpick a small section inside and measure the seam allowance. If it is 2 cm, you can usually let out about 1 cm per seam and keep 1 cm to hold it. Across two side seams, that is up to 4 cm more room.
On dark or shiny fabric, the old stitch holes may still show. Test on the inside, and tell the customer honestly before you start.
Fixing faults
Three common sewing faults
Check threading, use a new fine needle, and let the feed dogs move the fabric. Do not pull.
Change the needle. Use a ballpoint needle for knits. Check the flat side faces the right way.
Measure each leg, pin more closely, and press before stitching.
Customers judge you by small details. Puckering means the seam wrinkles. Check your threading, try a new fine needle, and let the machine move the fabric instead of pulling it.
Skipped stitches usually mean the needle. Change it, and use a ballpoint needle for knits. Most stitch faults come from the needle or threading, not the tension dial.
An uneven hem means one leg was not measured. For example, Grace checks four pairs of school trousers, finds one leg 1 cm longer, and re-hems it before the parent arrives.

Seams straight, locked, no puckering
Both sides match within about 0.5 cm
Raw edges finished
Fastenings work ten times
Threads trimmed, chalk gone, pressed
Check every job against this list. Even, balanced stitches. Straight, locked seams with no puckering. Both legs or sleeves matching within about half a centimetre.
Raw edges finished. Buttons and zips opening and closing smoothly ten times. Loose threads trimmed, chalk removed, and the garment pressed. Press means lift and set down the iron, not slide it.
Job number, date in, name and phone
Work agreed and measurements
Condition notes, like stains
Price, deposit and balance
Most quarrels come from unclear instructions, missed dates and price. A job card prevents them. Write the job number, date, and the customer's name and phone.
Write the work agreed and the measurements.
Note any existing damage, and tell the customer.

Agree the price before starting, and record the deposit and balance. Before releasing a garment, confirm the money has arrived in your own bank or wallet app, not from the customer's phone screen. Fake alerts are common.
Give a realistic collection date. Keep measurements private, and ask before taking or posting any photo.

Many beginner tailors guess their prices, or copy the cheapest person on the street. Then they work hard and have nothing left.

The four parts
Materials the job uses
Labour: your time per hour
Profit, often 20 to 30%
A price must cover four things. First, materials: the zip, thread, buttons. Count only what this job uses. One reel of thread does many jobs.
Second, labour. That is the minutes you spend, times a fair value for your time per hour. Use the same hourly value every time.

Third, running costs: fuel or electricity, needles, oil, data, transport. Add them for a month and divide by your usual number of jobs. For example, about 12,000 naira a month across about 60 jobs is about 200 naira per job.
Fourth, profit, often 20 to 30% for small service work. Profit is not your pay. Your pay is already in labour. Profit lets you save, replace tools and grow.

Materials: zip and thread
Labour: 45 minutes
Profit at 20%
Naira prices are approximate.
For example, Funke repairs clothes from home in Abeokuta. These prices are approximate, so use your own market prices.
Materials: the zip is 500 naira and thread about 50, so 550 naira.
Labour: about 45 minutes. At 1,500 naira an hour, that is 1,125 naira.
Running costs share: about 200 naira. So her total cost is 1,875 naira.
Profit at 20% adds 375 naira.
Her price comes to 2,250 naira. Nearby tailors charge between 2,000 and 3,000, so she rounds to 2,500. She knows she is not working at a loss.
Price rules
Charge fairly, never at a loss
Do
Charge extra for same-day work
Small discount for bulk jobs
Write prices as "from" a figure
Time each job and write it down
Do not
Discount below your total cost
Undercut a neighbour to win
Release a garment before payment
Charge extra for same-day work, because it pushes other jobs back. A small discount for bulk work, like ten school trousers for one family, is fine.
Write prices as from a figure, so you can charge more for difficult fabrics. And time your jobs. You will get faster.
Never discount below your total cost. If you undercut a neighbour, you lose money on every job. Compete on quality, speed and reliability instead.
And check every transfer in your own app before handing over the garment.
Show your work
Before-and-after photos that sell
Ask permission before any on-body photo or post
Daylight near a window, no flash
Plain sheet or plain wall
Same angle for before and after
Close-up of the repair itself
Label with the job number
A clear before-and-after photo does more selling than any message. Shoot in daylight near a window, or in shade. Avoid flash.
Lay the garment on a plain sheet, or hang it against a plain wall.
Take the before and after photos from the same angle and distance.
Add a close-up of the zip, the hem stitching or the patch.
Label each photo with the job number. For on-body photos, ask permission first, and crop out the face unless she agrees.
Finding customers
Free profile, catalogue with photos and "from" prices, quick replies and chat labels.
Schools, dry cleaners, clothing sellers and community groups see damaged clothes often.
Meet in daylight, tell someone where you are going, never post your home address.
Set up WhatsApp Business. It is free. Add a clear profile, a catalogue item for each service with a photo and a from price, and quick replies for your price list.
Look for partners. For example, Patience in Port Harcourt shows her photos to a dry cleaner and collects repairs twice a week. She gets steady work without advertising.
When you collect or deliver clothes, meet in daylight in a public or familiar place, tell someone at home where you are going, and give your address only to confirmed customers.
